title: What the homepage has to prove for a small consultancy
metaTitle: What a small consultancy homepage must prove
excerpt: Name the problem you actually take, then offer a working session. A list of industries tells a buyer they might as well do the work themselves.
alt: A cream sofa between two bright windows, with a framed abstract painting and teal vases, a tasteful room that does not name the problem a consultancy should lead with.
caption: A handsome room is not the problem the buyer is stuck on. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a small consultancy homepage prove first?
faqs.answer: Name the problem you take, in the buyer's words, and offer a working session that produces a decision. A buyer comparing you with doing it themselves already knows their industry. They are checking whether this problem is one you will actually finish.

faqs.question: Why is a list of industries a weak hero?
faqs.answer: It tries to look like range, and it reads as the absence of a problem. The buyer then assumes your method is generic, which is what they already have in-house. Name the setting only when it changes the work, as part of the problem sentence, not as a badge row.

faqs.question: What makes a working session real on the page?
faqs.answer: Say how long it is, what they leave holding, who must attend, and what it is not. If you cannot define those four, the button is a vague call. Do not offer two different sessions in the first screen.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A small consultancy homepage has one job for a buyer who is comparing you with doing the work themselves: name the problem you actually take, and offer a way to book a working session. A list of industries does not do that. It tells them you are available to many sectors, which is exactly the reason they think they might as well keep the problem in-house. Nielsen Norman Group's research puts a clock on the correction. People often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and the first 10 seconds decide whether they stay. If those seconds are a row of sector names, the buyer has already filed you with the generalists.

Write the page in that order. The problem first, in their words. Then the session: what they will leave holding, how long it is, and what they should bring. Everything else can wait. The average visit lasts a little less than a minute, and people have time to read only about a quarter of the words. The first screen is the argument that hiring you is safer than another month of doing it themselves.

## The problem, then the session

The problem is a job, not a market. "We untangle pricing for product companies whose quotes still live in a spreadsheet" is a problem. "We partner with leaders across technology, healthcare, and consumer" is a tour of the economy. The buyer who might do it themselves already knows their industry better than you do. They do not need you to list it. They need to see a problem they have postponed, described tightly enough that doing it alone looks slower.

The session is the action. "Book a working session" is an action if the next screen says what the session is. "Learn more" is a hallway. "Contact" is a hallway with a form. The label should match a real block of time in which a decision gets made, not a chemistry call that exists to qualify them.

Put both in the first view on a phone. One sentence for the problem. One button for the session. One picture of the work, not of a tasteful room. If you have a true boundary, one line can sit beside the button. "We do not stay on as a fractional team." "We stop at the decision, and your staff does the rollout." A boundary is a gift to someone comparing you with their own calendar. It shows the engagement will end.

Do not open with a mission. The buyer is not choosing a worldview. They are choosing whether this Tuesday's problem is still theirs. Google's helpful-content guidance asks whether a reader leaves knowing enough to take the next step. A mission paragraph does not book a session. A problem sentence can.

## Why a list of industries fails this buyer

An industry list is how a small firm tries to look larger. It reassures the partners that no lead will feel excluded. The buyer reads it as a lack of a problem. If you serve ten sectors, they assume the method is generic, and generic is what they already have in a template, a board deck, or a smart colleague.

The list also invites the wrong comparison. A founder in a clinic does not hire you because you have a clinic logo. They hire you if the problem, a scheduling mess, a pricing mess, a positioning mess, is one you have decided before, and if the session will force a decision they have been avoiding. The logo is optional. The decision is not.

There is a narrow exception. If the problem only exists in one setting, name that setting as part of the problem, not as a badge. "Pricing for single-location clinics that still quote by phone" is a problem with a place in it. "Healthcare, and also logistics, and also SaaS" is a badge row. Keep the place when it changes the work. Drop it when it is only a claim of range.

If you truly take three problems, say the three problems. Do not hide them under industries. A buyer with one problem should be able to see it and ignore the other two. An industry grid makes them do the sorting. They will not. They will go back to the spreadsheet.

## How to name the problem

Use the sentence the buyer uses when they complain, not the sentence you use in a proposal.

"We still don't know what to charge." "The founder is still in every deal." "The site lists everything we have ever done." Those are problems. "Go-to-market strategy" and "organizational effectiveness" are shelves. Shelves are where this buyer expects to waste a quarter.

Write one sentence with three parts. Who has the problem. What is stuck. What done looks like, in their hands, not in your deliverable taxonomy. "A founder-led company leaves the session with a price list they can send, and a list of deals they will stop discounting." That is done. "A strategic roadmap" is not done. They cannot hold a roadmap against the option of doing it themselves this weekend.

Add the negative. What you will not take. A negative is how a DIY buyer trusts the positive. If you will not facilitate a staff offsite, say so. If you will not produce a fifty-page deck, say so. The thing you refuse is often the thing they were afraid they would be paying for.

Test the sentence on someone who has the problem and has not hired you. Give them ten seconds. If they say "consulting," the sentence is still a category. Narrow it until they name the stuck thing. You want fewer inquiries. You want the inquiries to be the problem you take.

## What the working session must be

Define the session on the homepage in four facts, or do not use the words.

How long. What they leave with. Who from their side must be in the room. What it is not. Ninety minutes. A decision written in their words. The person who can say yes. Not a discovery that leads to a proposal for a discovery.

If you cannot define it, the button is a lie, and a buyer comparing you with their own time will feel the lie immediately. They are protective of the calendar. A vague session looks like the meeting they already know how to run, which means they do not need you.

Price can be a sentence if you are willing to say the shape. "The session is a fixed fee. Longer work, if any, is scoped after." If the session is unpaid, say that too, and say what you will not do for free. Do not hide the shape and hope the button carries it. The next page can hold the detail. The homepage has to hold the truth.

Do not offer two sessions in the hero. "Book a call" and "book a workshop" split the buyer the way two buttons split a recruiting site. Pick the session that matches the problem. The other can be a text link after they have seen the problem.

## What can wait below the first screen

Under the first view, teach the person who stayed. How the session runs, in the order of the hour. One story: the constraint, the decision, the problem, not a logo. What you will not do after the session, so they can see the edge. Who is in the room from your side, by name and by the problem they take.

Skip the industry wall. Skip a counter of clients. Skip a carousel of sectors "we understand." Each of those reintroduces the failure the hero just avoided. If a proof mentions a sector, it should be because the constraint was specific to that place, and the decision should still be the point.

A useful order:

1. The problem, with two examples of the stuck state.
2. The session, hour by hour, including what you need them to bring.
3. One decision you forced that they would have delayed.
4. Who does the work.
5. The session again.

Each block should add a fact. Repeating "we roll up our sleeves" is not a fact. The buyer who might do it themselves has sleeves. They need a reason those sleeves are the wrong ones for this problem.

## A test with someone who might do it themselves

Find a founder or operator who has the problem and has been solving it on weekends. Show them the page on a phone for about ten seconds. Hide it. Ask what problem the firm takes, and what they would be booking. If they say "consulting" and "a call," the page has not proved either thing.

Then leave the page open and ask whether they would still do it themselves. Listen for the industry list, the word "strategic," and any session that sounds like a tour of your method. Change the sentence. Do not add a paragraph below to repair an opening that failed. People who leave in the first 10 seconds do not scroll to your method.

Three people are enough if they miss the same thing. If two of them think the session is a sales call, rename it or change what it contains. If two of them name a problem you do not want, you have been too broad in order to look busy. Narrow it. The cost is fewer wrong sessions. That cost is the point.

## When the homepage is still a directory of sectors

A few patterns remain after the first honest test.

The firm takes many problems and will not choose. The page becomes a directory. Choose the problem this site is for. Let other problems live on inner pages with their own sentences, or stop offering them. The firm is proud of range and keeps a row of industry names under a good problem sentence. Delete the row. The sentence was working. The row undoes it. The firm has a real session and describes it as "let's hop on a call." Replace the verb before you rewrite the headline again.

If the first screen names the problem and the session, the next question is the fee. A buyer comparing you with their own time will look for the price as soon as the problem feels familiar. Read [how to show the shape of the fee](/blog/a-pricing-page-for-a-small-consultancy) before you hide it behind the booking button.

If you want to pressure-test that first screen with someone who builds pages for a living, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the problem sentence you are willing to say in public. The call is a working session on that sentence, not a tour of sectors.
